title: Lalita's city: the Sri Yantra
hookLine: the goddess rises from a fire, and her chariot and city become a drawing people worship
carry: a yantra is the goddess's home, in shape
tomorrow: who comes first, Shiva or the goddess?

cards: The gods are losing. A demon named Bhanda, born, in the story, from the ashes of the god of love, has taken their worlds. So they build a great fire and offer into it the last thing they have: themselves.
And out of the flames rises the goddess Lalita, radiant, smiling, armed. This is the Lalitopakhyana, told in the Brahmanda Purana.
A city is raised for her, and she rides out to war on a chariot called Chakraraja, the king of wheels. So why would a goddess's chariot end up as a drawing on a home shrine, with flowers on it?

teach.h: THE SRI YANTRA: TRIANGLES AROUND A DOT.

teach.b: The Sri Yantra, also called the Sri Chakra, is the goddess's great yantra: triangles pointing up and down, woven through each other around a single dot, rings of petals, a square frame with a gate on each side.

teach.h: HER CHARIOT, HER CITY, IN SHAPE.
teach.b: In Sri Vidya, the tradition that worships the goddess as Lalita, many read it as her chariot and her city at once.
Her thousand names, the Lalita Sahasranama, which many families chant, praise her as born from the fire of consciousness, riding the king of wheels. Here's the teaching.
If a mantra is the deity in sound, a yantra is the deity in shape. Not a picture of her face, but a map of her presence, a place she's invited to dwell. So worship moves the way you'd enter her city.
It starts at the outer square, at the gates, and travels inward, ring by ring, through the petals and the triangles, to the dot at the center, the bindu.

teach.h: THE BINDU: SHIVA AND SHAKTI, ONE.
teach.b: There, tradition says, Shiva and the goddess are one. The flowers aren't for ink or copper. They're for the one the lines make a home for.
To worship it is to walk from the edge of the world to its center, and find her already there.

how: In Sri Vidya worship, the goddess is worshipped in the Sri Yantra, with offerings that move from the outer square toward the central dot.

games.why: the worship walks from the edge inward, through petals and triangles, to the bindu, where tradition says Shiva and the goddess are one.

practice: If you have a yantra or a sacred image at home, let your eyes start at its outer edge and move inward slowly, a ring with each breath, until you reach its center. Rest there.
If you don't, any pattern near you, a tile, the weave of a sleeve, can carry your eyes the same way, edge to center.

wordCard.voice: What tantra actually is: here, worship of a yantra, the goddess in shape, walked from the gates in to the center dot.

orig.note: Sanskrit yantra; in tantric worship, a diagram that is a deity's form in shape.

carryVoice: For the road: a yantra is the goddess's home, in shape. Lalita's city fits on a copper plate. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Lalitopakhyana, Brahmanda Purana (the demon Bhanda, born from the ashes of Kama; the gods offer themselves into a great fire; Lalita rises from it, builds her city and rides the chariot Chakraraja against Bhanda)
Lalita Sahasranama (names praising her as born from the fire-pit of consciousness, chidagni-kunda-sambhuta, and mounted on the chariot Chakraraja)
Saundarya Lahari, verse 11 (the Sri Chakra as the goddess's dwelling: triangles of Shiva and of Shakti)
Sri Vidya worship of the Sri Yantra (outer square with gates, petal rings, interlocking triangles, central bindu; worship from the outside inward)
